planting.note: Set dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; this selection fruits only on primocanes, so the first-year planting can produce a crop the same season under good growing conditions.

directions: Released from the University of Arkansas breeding program under the designation APF-122, Mary Carmen is a moderately thorny, primocane-only fruiting blackberry notable for ripening three to four weeks ahead of other primocane cultivars in the program. Its erect canes carry less vegetative vigor than many Arkansas releases, which cuts down on the summer tipping and lateral management that bushier types demand. Berries are medium-sized, glossy black, and consistently well shaped with good flavor and strong shelf life. Because fruiting is confined to current-season growth, mow or cut canes to the ground each winter rather than managing separate floricane and primocane crops.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant dormant, certified virus-free canes in early spring; Kelly fruits on second-year floricanes and ripens early in the Arkansas lineup, ahead of midseason types like Ouachita.

directions: Patented by the University of Arkansas as selection A-2454T, Kelly is an early-season, floricane-fruiting blackberry prized for medium-sized, very firm berries with a sweet, subacid flavor and good postharvest handling. Plants have shown reliable health and vigor in Arkansas trials, making this a straightforward addition to an early-harvest lineup. Grow on a simple two-wire trellis in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, removing spent floricanes immediately after harvest. Thin and tip primocanes in midsummer so next year's fruiting canes branch well and stay manageable.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Set dormant thornless canes in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; expect rapid row establishment and a usable primocane crop in the first year under favorable conditions.

directions: Blakely is a thornless, primocane-fruiting blackberry from the University of Arkansas, bred as selection APF-238T from a cross involving the earlier release APF-77. It is valued for its early ripening, sweet flavor with pleasing aromatics, and glossy, uniformly round, medium-sized fruit produced on both erect primocanes and floricanes. Plants grow vigorously and establish quickly after planting, so give them a trellis and room to fill in. Remove floricanes after the early summer harvest and tip primocanes in midsummer to set up a strong fall crop.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; Amanda ripens early in the floricane season and performs well in both fresh-market and small-garden plantings.

directions: Developed by the University of Arkansas as selection A-2491T from a cross involving 'Natchez', Amanda is a floricane-fruiting blackberry known for large berries with good sub-acid flavor, strong postharvest handling, and consistently high yields. Breeders also noted excellent plant health alongside its early-season ripening, making it a dependable addition where disease pressure is a concern. Grow in full sun on a trellis in well-drained, fertile soil, cutting spent floricanes to the ground right after harvest. Thin and tip the new primocanes through the summer to build strong fruiting wood for the following year.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Set dormant thornless canes in early spring; Danna is among the earliest-fruiting primocane blackberries in the Arkansas program and can produce a usable crop the first season.

directions: Patented in 2023 as APF-409T from the University of Arkansas breeding program, Danna is a thornless, primocane-fruiting blackberry bred for extremely early and precocious cropping, bearing its first fruit in mid-July in Arkansas trials. The berries are above average in size, very firm, and resist softening after rain, giving growers a dependable, weather-tolerant crop for fresh market or individually quick frozen packing. Floricanes are winter hardy to roughly -10 degrees Celsius and need around 200 hours of winter chill to crop well the following spring. Train the vigorous, erect canes to a simple trellis in full sun, removing spent floricanes after harvest and managing primocanes for a strong fall flush where the season allows double-cropping.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
